headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid spy scandal, prompting tighter US chip export rules
dek: Jensen Huang stepped down after allegations of Chinese espionage and chip smuggling, leading Congress to pursue stricter AI chip export controls[S1][S2][S4].
what_happened: Nvidia co‑founder and CEO Jensen Huang stepped down after a series of controversies that surfaced in late 2025 and early 2026[S1][S2][S3].
Congress seeks stricter AI chip export limits after Nvidia spy scandal, urging Nvidia executives to testify[S4].
Pony.ai is using mid‑tier compute and Chinese‑made chips to offset Nvidia supply limits[S5].

sections.title: Jensen Huang leaves Nvidia amid scandals
paragraphs: Nvidia co‑founder and CEO Jensen Huang stepped down after a series of controversies that surfaced in late 2025 and early 2026[S1][S2][S3]. The New York Times first reported a Chinese spy plot involving Huang on October 29, 2025, and subsequent reporting linked him to alleged chip‑smuggling and personal misconduct[S1][S2][S3].
Singapore authorities confiscated her passport in June 2025 and barred her from the country after she gave inaccurate information to police[S1][S2][S3].

The Biden administration has restricted sales of Nvidia’s top‑tier chips to China to preserve AI superiority, and any perceived compromise of Nvidia’s leadership raises national‑security concerns[S1][S2][S3]. Huang’s public persona, once compared to Steve Jobs, had become intertwined with the company’s market dominance, so his exit could affect investor confidence and the broader AI supply chain[S1][S2].

sections.title: Congress wants to tighten export rules on AI chips after Nvidia spy scandal
paragraphs: After revelations about Jensen Huang’s ties to a suspected Chinese spy, Congress is pursuing tighter export controls on AI chips[S4]. Both Democrats and Republicans have voiced support for new measures and have asked Nvidia leaders to testify before lawmakers[S4].

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said Huang and the Trump administration must answer to Congress, while Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott sent letters to Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick requesting public testimony[S4]. Bills such as the Remote Access Security Act, first introduced in the House in April 2025, are gaining renewed interest despite earlier Senate stalls[S4]. House Speaker Mike Johnson expressed a “growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China” and personally supports restricting China’s access to powerful AI chips from companies like Nvidia[S4].

sections.title: Pony.ai shifts to domestic chips amid Nvidia export concerns
paragraphs: The company said demand for Nvidia chips exceeds supply and that it will use lower‑cost compute and more locally made processors for training its self‑driving models[S5].

Leo Wang, Pony.ai’s CFO, explained that engineers are now instructed to maximise efficiency, often opting for mid‑tier compute resources rather than top‑tier Nvidia GPUs[S5]. He added that the firm is increasing its reliance on domestically produced chips, which have received growing attention and development in recent years[S5]. Wang believes this domestic option provides flexibility and helps close the performance gap caused by limited Nvidia supply[S5].

Nvidia supplies AI processors for both running autonomous‑driving software and training the underlying models, making it a cornerstone of the global self‑driving ecosystem[S5]. Recent political fallout and possible export restrictions could reduce Chinese access to these chips, prompting companies like Pony.ai to diversify their hardware sources[S5].

sections.title: AI tools boost ransomware tactics
paragraphs: Researchers report a rise in ransomware incidents as attackers incorporate artificial intelligence into their methods[S6]. The number of alleged attacks on public leak sites reached nearly 3,000 over the summer, a 20‑40 % increase since spring[S6]. Experts say the growth is driven by more international campaigns, with the United States remaining steady but still high[S6].

The surge is linked to AI use in parts of the ransomware chain, such as crafting more convincing phishing emails and automating negotiation messages[S6]. Allan Liska of Recorded Future notes that while most groups remain human‑run, they are experimenting heavily with large language models, which could accelerate changes in tactics[S6]. Cynthia Kaiser, former FBI cyber deputy director, highlights that the international dimension of attacks is the most novel aspect and attributes part of the increase to AI‑enabled capabilities[S6].

Ransomware has been a top cyber threat for a decade, targeting institutions and indirectly affecting individuals[S6]. This shift mirrors broader trends where AI is used to automate social‑engineering attacks across the cybercrime ecosystem[S6].

sections.title: AI‑driven air traffic tool sparks safety debate
paragraphs: On September 27 US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced the AI‑infused air‑traffic management system called SMART on X, calling it a “GAME CHANGER” and saying it would save time and cut delays[S7]. Three weeks later, on Friday the 13th, the FAA issued a national groundstop that disrupted airline schedules, and officials said there was no evidence of a cyberattack or that SMART caused the communications failure[S7]. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said officials could not yet rule out an AI fault[S7].

The SMART system is part of a broader AI aviation push, illustrated by a pilotless 3,200‑mile Cessna Caravan flight that departed Buchanan Field Airport in Concord, California and landed at Dare County Regional Airport in North Carolina, stopping at Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina and Fort Worth en route[S7]. Joby Aviation reported a safety pilot remained aboard but never intervened, marking a milestone for unmanned commercial flight[S7]. The flight navigated busy airspace and avoided storms without human control, showing AI can handle complex routing tasks[S7].

Air traffic control has traditionally relied on proven, human‑centric technology because safety is paramount[S7]. Recent AI introductions aim to improve efficiency, but industry veterans warn that rapid, untested changes could introduce new risks[S7]. The mixed reaction reflects a tension between potential economic benefits and concerns over reliability and safety in a sector that historically favors caution[S7].

card.hook: FAA groundstop sparks AI safety fears[S7].
points: The FAA halted all flights nationwide after a communications glitch[S7].
Officials can’t rule out the new AI system SMART as the cause[S7].
card.take: Watch for schedule changes and demand transparency on AI use in air traffic[S7].
card.angle: AI‑driven air‑traffic tool may be behind a nationwide flight halt, raising safety concerns for travelers.

why_it_matters.text: Chinese autonomous‑vehicle maker Pony.ai is shifting to domestically produced chips to avoid potential Nvidia export restrictions, illustrating how geopolitical tensions can force companies to redesign hardware strategies and affect product timelines[S5].
